Palworld gives you options ... whether you die and lose your items or not;  how much daylight and night you want; gives you many options to breed pals and; most of all since I'm an elderly and had a stoke, it allows the option to make the fight less difficult.

This is not "Pokémon with guns", this is Ark Survival Evolved with Pokémon. If you like survival/crafting games and like monster catching games, there is nothing better on the market than Palworld, period. 

This comes from someone who has been playing Pokémon since generation 1. It came out when I was in middle school and I have played every mainline game and most of the side games. I'm still a fan of Pokémon, but this is such a fresh take on the monster catching genre that Gamefreak has a ton of catching up to do. 

I also have over 1000 hours in ARK and Survival Evolved. I played it mostly in the first few years of it's life. All the base building and creature systems in Palworld are leagues better than ARK in every conceivable way. It's unknown if ARK 2 is still happening, but it now has a really high bar to live up to.

---------------------------------------

10 tips for new players to make your experience more enjoyable:

1. Catch 5 of every Pal. You'll know you've caught your 5 when the icon to the right of a wild pal's name goes from white to yellow. This rewards you with an effigy (see #5).

2. Follow the MSQ (Main Story Quest). It'll lead you naturally from area to area by the levels of the pals in that area. The MSQ also unlocks the towers (gym leaders) as you progress through it, which unlocks specific nodes in the tech tree that you will need.

3. Put your stat points in Weight and Stamina first. I put every point in weight until I got to 2000, then put the rest in Stamina. Weight increases your carry capacity which is super important for farming heavy rarer ores and Stamina allows you to sprint and mine longer without getting tired, Stamina also effects the pals you are riding.

4. Get a few Vixy's early (little white & brown dog/fox guy), build a Ranch (unlocked at level 5), put them in it. Passive money, arrow and palsphere generation.

5. Build a Statue of Power as soon as possible (unlocked at level 9) and make sure you feed all the pal effigies that you find into it to give your player some extra passive stats. Most effigies are found on the overworld, they look like little glowing pal statues on a pedestal and there are 12 different types. Different areas have different effigies.

6. Do every active dungeon that you come across (the caves with a blue glowy aura), they have tons of good things inside from pals and rare materials to blueprints and pal upgrade materials and more. Some of them are even just single-room treasure rooms.

7. As soon as you unlock your 2nd base, use it as an iron farming base and fill it with good mining pals. Iron Ore is the basis for everything from that point on and you will need tons of it for; higher level palshpheres, weapons, ammo, armor, accessories, base building materials and more.

8. Feed your Pals! You will need a ton of food for your pals, especially as you unlock additional bases and have more and more pals deployed and doing tasks. Check each base periodically and makes sure they don't run out of food or the pals will get bad debuffs that are detrimental and are a bit of a pain to cure. Cooked food is better than non-cooked. Have at least half a base dedicated to farming food.

9. Unlock the Guild Chest at level 41 and put one in each of your bases. These chests have a large storage capacity and all share the same inventory, so put your most used crafting materials inside of them so you have access to all of them from all of your bases!

10. Have fun and go at your own pace! There is so much to do in Palworld. Rotate your time between; working on your bases, going out and exploring the world, catching some new pals, doing some dungeons, battling some bosses, doing the main story quest and just living your best Palworld Life.

--------------------------------------------------

541 hours so far and i just want to do a review even though the game is still in early access. 

Palworld has been incredibly entertaining for someone like me who is constantly looking for good survival games. Many games leave a lot to be desired when it comes to inventory management, base building and accessibility for people who want to play with different settings.

Palworld has a ton of potential to be a game capable of nailing all 3, from the simplistic design and gameplay that feeds very well into the survival aspect, to the many settings allowing you to adjust grind and pace of the experience. Endgame consists of perfecting your favorite pals, amassing a ton of loot and fighting difficult Raid bosses. That being said, there are still some very unpleasant experiences waiting to be had.

- Endgame Raids are tuned for groups and min-maxed pals. Expect to spend weeks breeding and perfecting stats/IV's/Traits on a specific meta pal for that Raid boss just to be able to beat them alone. Newest raid bosses/Oil rigs are difficulty sponges, add more damage and health. Oil rigs alone are very unrewarding with drop chances for legendary weapons being abnormally low, and loot from oil rig enemies is pathetic so most people end up rushing through them. It's pretty bad.

- No options for speeding up breeding/altering RNG of traits being transferred. Breeding is a HUGE part of palworlds progression, and while you can technically complete all bosses without breeding, it is very hard to do so and most End-Game bosses demand you have at least a maxed souls/IV's pal team at level cap. Breeding can take days to get what you want and its all up to RNG.

- Base building is very unpolished. Expect frequent frustration as you have difficulty placing down items as they find random invisible objects underground preventing you from building there. You cannot multi-build, have fun placing 20 pillars down individually every 3 tiles away to create solid support for structures if you hate the clunkiness and uncertainty of building on ground. No Cross hatching or triangle pieces either, enjoy making a square fort in a circular radius of your base.

- Nintendo. Probably affecting this game in the most negative way possible. Due to a lawsuit that nintendo threw at palworld, many features are currently at risk, or have been removed. Gliding is currently patented by nintendo, no more riding your glider pals. You can no longer release your pals by throwing them out due to nintendo patenting the throwing mechanic, making releasing your pals very clunky. Thankfully palworld was able to fix it up to be much more tolerable. So far nintendo has been a huge roadblock for palworld over petty jealousy of being very successful with mechanics that pokemon uses. Instead of letting palworld flourish into an amazing game, they are trying to burry it in the dirt and prevent anyone from switching to a pokemon alternative. If that doesn't scream a big "Fuck You" to people who want to enjoy a fun game then i don't know what will. Sorry, i could rant on about nintendos actions for so long, it really is depressing.

So far i would give this game a 9/10 for potential in early access. The only reason i didn't give that 10/10 was due to those weird ass decisions to make drop rates for crucial work books/blueprints below 1% for dropping, and the inflated difficulty of the new Oil rigs/Raid bosses, making them incredibly tedious to beat with very little reward. I question pawlorlds future balance choices for upcoming content. Pro tip; if you're struggling with the endgame Raid bosses, just turn damage up to max ( x10 multiplier ) and get a team of max condensed Gobfins and an elemental buff mount that the raid boss is weak to. Pray you can get at least a tier 3 or above multi guided missle launcher and go nuts on it. Don't feel bad, the fights are not difficult, they just demand you put in weeks to breed perfected min/maxed pals, have a meta build with legendary rarity weapons and cooperate with 1 or more players to take it down reliably. That level of breeding is not for everyone, and it burnt me out multiple times. Settings are a godsend and they are adding more every update!

When I first played Legends: Arceus, I thought it was the best Pokemon game ever. It had most of the "this is what a perfect Pokemon game" features: big, open worlds, riding Pokemon, reasons to explore and discovering brand new things.

But then I played Palworld and realized: THIS is the best Pokemon game ever. Pokemon's biggest flaws (in my opinion) and how Palworld solves them:

* The majority of Pokemon are functionally useless. Whether it's stats, move pools, or typing, the majority of Pokemon aren't viable. Every Pal has some benefit, whether it's in your base or exploring in the world. And this has been further improved by...
* Your "favorite" Pokemon might actually be garbage. It sucks so much to finish a playthrough with Pokemon you've bonded with to then discover their IVs/EVs are terrible and will be of no use to use for endgame content. Over time, there have been SOME ways to "fix" your Pokemon, but it takes a lot of time and money. But you can now upgrade the "IVs" of any pal, increase their stats in multiple ways, and even change their "passives", gender,  and work suitability. You can make any individual pal "good" and be by your side the entire game if you so choose.
* There's no sense of mystery or discovery left in Pokemon. All the big Pokemon are shown in the marketing, but you already know what the other 1,000+ are going to be and what biomes they'll live in. But I love wandering in Palworld's forests or climbing mountains to see if I can spot distant islands in the oceans. I might discover a new subtype of pal in a dungeon or in a cave, or even a random egg I found. I truly don't know what I'm going to find, and the world has become even more lived in as they've updated it over the past few years.

Everyone has different ideas of what their "ideal" critter catching/rearing game should be, so things like tech trees, base building, and no evolutions might be hard nos for some people, and that's okay. But Palworld has all of those for me, and even more, like the ability to make random spawn worlds or "nuzlocke" rules. 

It's at the point that I look at new Pokemon games, its cities with three enterable buildings, evolution mechanics so obsure you HAVE to google them, and the same 30 Pokemon being used in endgame and wonder...why put up with that anymore? Why not instead play a game that lets me use whatever creatures I want, spend my time wherever I want, and always be excited to go out in the world? 

The fact that I already own the game and don't need to buy a Switch 2 is a great bonus lol

After more than 100 hours, I can confidently say this is the game every Pokémon fan has dreamed about since they were a kid.

Catching Pals, building your base, exploring the world, fighting bosses, automating tasks, creating the perfect team... there's always something to do. I log in thinking I'll play for 30 minutes, and before I know it, three hours have disappeared.

I catch myself at work, lying on the couch, or trying to fall asleep thinking, "I need to expand my base," "I should catch that Pal," or "Do I finally have enough resources for that project?" Palworld somehow lives rent-free in my head even when I'm not playing.

The progression is incredibly addictive, exploration constantly rewards your curiosity, and there are so many different ways to play that it never gets boring. It's fantastic solo, but with friends it's on a whole different level.

It's been a long time since a game kept me hooked for over 100 hours without ever feeling repetitive. There's always one more goal to chase, one more Pal to catch, one more upgrade to build, or one more adventure waiting around the corner.

I went in expecting this to be great and it still exceeded my expectations! I didn't once think about picking up another game and taking a break while I was playing through this.

+ Positives:

+ I know a lot of people make comparisons to Pokemon and while yes there are some, I find Palworld is a lot more innovative with mechanics and feels more involved. This is so much more than just some pokemon wannabe clone. It's its own thing and it excels at most of what it does.
+ There is an astonishing amount of content to play through. The game is still EA and it took me 160 hours to get all achievements while also relaxing and just enjoying the game. Catching pals, crafting, breeding, boss fights, gathering, mining, dungeon exploration as well as a big world to explore. You can ride some pals, fly on some pals or put some on your shoulder so they can be the cutest killing machines who field a machine gun and fight with you.
+ Breeding feels very in depth and you can lose hours if you fall into the rabbit hole of trying to breed with specific traits onto a pal. 
+ The game can offer a challenge when it comes to boss fights. While the first few are pretty simple, the later ones can be a little difficult even on normal difficulty, and take preparation. It's fun working to put together your little super team to beat those bosses you got your ass kicked by. 
+ If a challenge isn't your thing, there are world settings that will make it an easier experience. There's also a lot of options in general that allow you to change drop rates, capture chance etc. On the flip side, you can also make it extremely tough if that's your thing!
+ The summoned bosses are a lot of fun! Difficult and take preparation, but feels great when you see their defeat. 
+ Love the pal designs! Some of them must have taken a great deal of imagination with design and description. 

- Negative: 

- Tower bosses are scaled to how many people enter, but I do strongly believe the oil rigs are not. The last one doesn't feel balanced for a solo player, and instead feels like it was created with a team of four in mind. Can require some cheese tactics to get it done without getting completely obliterated.

Despite the memes of "its pokemon with guns!", it is in fact...Not Pokemon. Are there cute, cuddly creatures to collect? Yes! Can you catch them in a portable device? Also yes! But the actual meat and bones of this game is BY FAR more akin to the gameplay loop of ARK than anything Pokemon has pumped out ever. I prefer to describe it to my friends as "ARK with a Pokemon mod added to it" because that's how it plays. 

And I, obviously with my 600+ hours at the time of writing this, adore this game. I love the quirks, the replayability, the fact that Pocket Pair listens to their players! Every update, big or small, has been free. Which when they are delivering DLC sized updates other devs would have made you pay for? That is invaluable. 1.0 is on the horizon, and I cannot wait. (Except I actually can, please Pocket Pair, if you read these reviews, don't try to crunch 1.0 out as fast as possible. Take your time, make sure it comes out right. We can wait.)

The literal ONLY complaint I honestly have at this point (besides small QoL nags), is the fact modding is still quite buggy. I am extremely happy that the steam workshop finally works with Palworld, but holy nuts, I have run into 90% of my issues in the game just trying to get the game to work while modded. (Go figure, adding unstable mods to an early access game, which by nature is also unstable. I am boo boo the fool.)

Much like it's character designs, Palworld is a reconstituted frankenstein stitching together of ideas from six different sources at the same time, Pokemon, Ark, Breath Of The Wild, Fortnite, probably a few others I'm forgetting at the moment.

The weirdest part about this arrangement, is that it's actually good. It hasn't got a single original thought rolling around inside its little empty skull, but it's polished and fun and leans into the inherent comedy of its concept with success. It has also managed to sidestep the usual pitfalls of early access open world releases by both running with solid and stable performance and actually having a substantive amount of content on launch.

By all accounts, Palworld should be a disastrous mess, but somehow it is not. It's sheer recombinatory logic somehow manages to arrive at something compelling.

I went into Palworld expecting a novelty survival game with a gimmick. What I got instead was one of the most unexpectedly addictive, confident, and genuinely fun games I have played in years.

Palworld does something rare: it understands why survival games are fun and then refuses to bog that fun down with tedium. Gathering, crafting, base-building, and automation all feel purposeful. Nothing exists just to waste your time. The moment-to-moment loop is clean, readable, and rewarding, whether you are chopping trees, expanding a base, or watching your Pals efficiently run an operation you built from scratch.

The Pals themselves are the heart of the game, and not just as collectibles. They are workers, fighters, tools, liabilities, and sometimes absolute idiots in the best possible way. Assigning them jobs, watching their personalities emerge through behavior, and occasionally rescuing them from situations entirely of their own making creates an emergent charm that cannot be faked. The game constantly generates small stories without ever announcing that it is doing so.

Combat is far better than it has any right to be. Gunplay, melee, and Pal abilities blend into encounters that feel chaotic but controllable. You are never just standing back watching numbers happen. You are actively positioning, reacting, and making decisions while your Pals do the same, often in ways that surprise you. Boss fights feel earned, not scripted, and victory usually comes from preparation and execution rather than brute force.

The open world is dense without being exhausting. Exploration feels rewarding because there is always something useful over the next ridge: a new Pal, a resource vein, a dungeon, or a reason to move your base somewhere smarter. Fast travel and map design respect your time, which is something many games in this genre fail to do.

What truly elevates Palworld, though, is its confidence. It knows exactly what kind of game it is. It is not embarrassed by its absurdity, nor is it sloppy with its systems. Beneath the humor and shock value is a surprisingly robust automation and progression framework that scratches the same itch as factory builders while remaining accessible to players who just want to explore and fight.

Yes, it is still evolving. Yes, there are rough edges. But the foundation is rock solid, and the fun is immediate and persistent. Palworld is not a meme, not a clone, and not a joke that went too far. It is a legitimately excellent game that respects player agency, rewards creativity, and remembers that games are supposed to be enjoyable.

Highly recommended, especially if you are tired of survival games that confuse friction with depth.

Palworld is an open-world creature-focused game with survival mechanics, and although this combination may seem overwhelming at first, the implementation truly takes advantage of every one of those aspects.
The creatures, called Pals in-game, are not only your adventure friends, that help you navigate through the world and fend off hostile Pals and other humans, but are also your workforce helpers. Granted they are well taken care of, they'll help you with brute-force work on your base, with stuff like harvesting and storing resources, building, and in-line manufacturing. Your Pals are an essential part of everything you'll do in your base, that's because they truly live with you and you'll actually see them most of the time, and it makes them feel part of the world in a way that recent Pokémon games don't accomplish as well. And more than that, they all have their own flair and personality, you can sense that not only in their character traits, but in every aspect of their behavior: their attack and idle animations, as well as how often they eat, rest, and choose to be aggressive or not.

The exploration in this game is also excellent, expect beautifully diverse vistas to go through and secrets to uncover. Most important of all, however, is that it's a fun thing to do, especially accompanied by your Pals. The world itself is well crafted and plentifully diverse, with points of interest scattered through it and region-specific Pals to be friendly or hostile with.
It's important to point out that this game's theme also has an edge to it, as you'll be dealing with actual guns in the late game, and your Pals can also use them or be used in one way or another in combat. So that may or may not be a deal-breaker for you, but I can't disagree that this game has its own charm and I can admit it's pretty funny.

The base building is pretty extensive in this game, as is the technology progression that you get through playing and levelling up. I can almost see it scratching the itch for a lite factory sim game with the way you can build production lines and automate farming, cooking, mining etc.

As for performance, I've tested this game in two systems, one fairly low-mid-range with a 4-core Intel CPU and an RTX 4060 and the game runs as well as it could realistically be expected for this config. What I think is odd is that there seems to be an engine limit or bottleneck of some kind, as it doesn't run as well as you'd expect in a high-end system I tested (Ryzen 5800X3D + RTX 5080), so don't expect obscenely high framerates, especially in indoor scenes on a larger complex base, even on lower settings. But most importantly it should run acceptably well on most systems, and the team being small and the game being an Unreal Engine game, I think it's a good result overall!

To conclude, Palworld deserves so much more than to live in the shadow of Pokémon. It can't be described solely as a ball-throwing, creature-catching game, it's more than that. The game is still in early access with a release looming on the horizon, so it has a lot to improve still, but as it is, it's an excellent game that I'll happily recommend to most, even if we were in a world where Pokémon games were still high quality.

Crafting: There is a exceptional crafting system here. It is extremely detailed like most games like this and it does very well in keeping you engaged for many many hours.

Gameplay: The game shines here. The game is literally all gameplay. Little to no cutscenes, no voice acting, just pure raw gameplay. Between the crafting systems, the building systems, the creature capturing, over 200 pals at the time of this review, different rare pals. Different type / versions of the same pals, weapon system, bows, guns, melee. This game literally has it all its insane. The amount of builds you can try is ridiculous. Each pal has a passive bonus to the party or when its mounted. There are multiple items you can equip a pal with, like guns, saddles etc. There is so much here and its where the game really shines.

Boss Battles / Alpha Hunting: The game offers the ability to fight and capture alpha versions of the same pals you find in the wild. It makes a fun experience to try to get as many alphas as possible. There is also legendary pals you can try to hunt as well. 

Dungeons: The game has pretty fun and a nice selection of diverse dungeons with items to farm inside and bosses to find. I do wish there was a little more to them as they just feel like extensions of the open world and nothing special really in their own right outside of materials you can only find in them. Still pretty fun.

Value: The game features an immense amount of value for a $30 retail video game. They kept the price the same at release of 1.0 and added so much content and fixes they couldnt even list the whole thing on steam. 

Cons:

Story: The story is palworld is fairly weak. Atleast the way its presented is weak. The game is obviously focused on its gameplay over anything else, which isnt bad for its addictive nature and how fun it is overall, but i wish there was more effort put into the story telling. 

Music: The game features barely any music. When the music does hit, its pretty nice. I just wish there was more. Especially when your in a dungeon. having it be super quiet just makes it feel like nothing special is happening. I dont know, I just feel like more music can be added here to really make the moments shine. Its lacking.

Glitches: The game is still filled with alot of glitches that pop up randomly. One of the most annoying ones was when an alpha pal i was trying to kill fell through the world and was still able to attack me but i couldnt do anything to them. After so much time in early access, this is unacceptable and needs to be worked on ASAP. 

Overall Palworld is everything I thought it would be and more. I purposefully waited for 1.0 before playing it and I am glad i did. This game is amazing and considering I have 56 hours in just a few days, i can see myself spending hundreds of hours in this.

I'll be honest, I decided to play this game purely for the memes. As a fan of Pokemon, when I caught wind of this new monster catching game where you can hand a "Pal" a sub-machine gun, I knew I had to check it out.

I've only owned Palworld for three days I've already almost played 10 hours which is a lot for me since I barely use my laptop for gaming. This game is still in early access but there's still a lot the game has to offer which is a given when it comes to these types of survival games. 

Palworld is a survival game similar to Ark: Survival Evolved, an open world game like The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, and a monster-catching game taking fairly heavy inspiration from Pokemon. You wake up on a desolate island and you gather materials to survive. The hook this time around is that you can do it with your Pals, this games collectible monsters. Its this mechanic that gets fleshed out throughout the game loop that really attaches me to it.

Survival base builder games aren't my favorite types of games, my closest experiences to compare to it would be something as basic as Minecraft and Terraria. The gameplay loop of gathering and building grows stale quick for me. This game streamlines the experience with how Pals you capture do those tedious tasks for you. Instead of me planting seeds, then watering, then harvesting, I can just have an elite group of Pals farm for me.

This game has numerous environments to experience: the usual old green forests, snowy mountain peaks, abandoned ruins, and much more. This all sounds fairly boring, but it's what's in the world that really makes it feel worth exploring. Climbing up mountain peaks often reward you with some eggs that can net you some rare late game Pals. In ruins, you can find resources to improve your Pal catching. Not to mention new Pals to find in each biome.

Then obviously, there is the monster catching aspect. This game reminds me of Pokemon Legends: Arceus when it comes to this. In Arceus, you can either capture Mons in the field phase or in the traditional battle phase. In Palworld, it doesn't have turn-based gameplay but it feels like the field gameplay has been more throughly explored compared to Pokemon Legends: Arceus. If you want to get a Pal you could just throw a sphere at them, or you can square up and beat'em to a pulp weakening them for capture. This brutality provides the game with an immersion unlike the entire Pokemon series. 

To round out this review, I implore you to give this game an honest try. Certainly the game has questionably unique designs, but looking past that grey area, this game shows a lot of promise. The way that Pocketpair implemented the Pals into almost every aspect of the game: from traversal, to battles, and even resource gathering, I can't help but be charmed by a few of Pals. My three favorite Pals are Daedream, Chillet, and Celaray. I give Palworld a solid 8 out of 10. They made a better open world Pokemon game than Pokemon. (I still do like Pokemon more though)

Now that 1.0 is out, it's a great time to update my review. Sad thing is, even after a couple major updates, collabs and 1.0, I don't have much new to say. It's an addictive gameplay loop and decent open world, I love how interactive the Pals are and I think Nintendo could learn a lot from how much this game lets them do to help you along and feel like part of the team even if they're not in your main party... but it still feels hollow.

As of release now, I think I can say definitively this game did not get better - it just got bigger. More critters, more areas, more bosses, more materials, more levels, more moves. Sadly, not much more polish at all. That was the part I really hoped they'd hammer on coming into 1.0, making the world feel more lived-in, giving us more story and memorable, bespoke challenges along the way. Maybe touch up some of the ugly bits, the edge cases with things like climbing, make some minigames or interactions a little friendlier and juicier, easier to pick up on and more enjoyable to do repeatedly. Aside from a handful more NPCs and small settlements (barely even villages, really) and some dedicated bases to break into (made out of the same toolset as player bases so they're a bit cramped and hard to navigate, and pal behavior gets wonky in them) I didn't get much added from my original wishlist. I still think the game's default settings are a grindy nightmare, but worse, even if you crank the droprate up there are still a few ores and special things that don't "drop" in the normal sense and so aren't affected and end up being a big bottleneck. I still hate that permadeath is only a toggle with no interactivity to it - either your Pals are immortal and just need a 10 minute nap to be back to perfect health, or the instant they hit 0 they're dead forever and a solid chunk of the game's potions and revives and medicine tools are fully useless, and things like raids are untouchable because they'll wipe an entire genetic lineage out of your collection in seconds.

So, overall, what I hoped were early access growing pains ended up being hardcoded features of the game going forward. The game is just bigger, longer, and has a handful more short cutscenes, still mostly to introduce bosses that you just teleport into unceremoniously. Aside from having an ending now, it still feels like early access to me. But I don't see any reason to assume the developer will do more than adding DLC later on (probably), and the community hasn't given an indication there's any interest in larger overhaul mods that might bring some of that vision I'd hoped to see to life.

In particular, the way I finished off that original review hurts, in context of what we got: 

>It feels like there's tons of potential here, especially with this game's massive viral success. Right now, it's a fun game, but not a fulfilling world that makes you want to be a part of it. A good survival game, good monster collecting game, good exploration and base building game, zero reason to stick in your mind once it's over except to think about how much you want to curl up with a Chillet. It could be so much more, but if future updates just push "this but more of it" then it'll always be just "good".

Palworld is a game that feels like less than the sum of its parts. It's cheapened by a lot of mechanics and ideas wholesale lifted from other games, but done much worse and with a less intentional hand making them feel tacked-on rather than deliberate and special. But even the things that work, don't feel like they fully cohere and come together to create something better. I fell in love with a lot of Pal designs, but the comradery and companionship eventually gives way to mechanics requiring stronger Pals and better passives, utility, etc. Combat is fun and I like the element of timing Pal switching as a sort of 'dodge' alongside watching your own health - yet the AI still breaks when a target is removed mid-attack and never tries to redirect to the next valid target, with few exceptions, so it feels like too much of an exploit in many cases. 

I can't find much that's outright broken, just a lot of ideas not given the proper time in the oven, coming out feeling half-baked or unfinished, pushed out functional and "good enough". It's missing a lot of whatever "special sauce" it is that makes a game from Nintendo somehow manage to feel like a journey despite being trounced by this game's graphics, scope/scale, and actual challenge.

Now that the story actually has an ending to it, I can say that it's acceptably climactic, with enough lead-up to make it feel somewhat earned. But it also feels like they did exactly as little as the game needed to not come across as unfinished. There's nothing memorable along the way, no big surprise, or unexpected shakeups. No characters to grow attached to, rivalries to form, character development to see (unless it's in the journal logs, which the devs care so little about, you have to dig through the escape menu to find the journals, rather than "hold X to view new journal" or a simple journal tab along with the inventory/map screens). It doesn't fall flat on its face, but mostly it feels like playing a cheap MMO story where it's there to be a mild framework to move you through the world and give you an excuse to do stuff along the way, and just wants to get itself out of the way so you can move on to the end-game content.

I'm coming away from Palworld mostly satisfied with the gameplay, enjoyed building bases and becoming stronger, seeing lots of cute and cool designs, but it's not going to stick with me. I wish I could give a more neutral recommendation, because there's still something fun to sink your teeth into there, but where I hoped a genuine large-scale pocket monster rival would come out of Palworld, I'm more convinced now that it's just about going through the motions and trying to challenge their merchandising and IP dominance. A functional game, but not much of a confident competitor.
